learningObjectives.title: Environmental impact and sustainability of food
Food security, sustainable diets and reducing food waste
Food processing and production (primary and secondary)
The effect of processing and fortification on food

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'food miles'?
options: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed
The number of shops a food is sold in before purchase
The energy used to cook a food at home
The weight of packaging used to transport a food
questions.explain: Food miles measure the distance food is transported from producer to consumer, which affects its carbon footprint.

questions.q: A food's 'carbon footprint' is a measure of what?
options: The greenhouse gases produced during its production, transport and storage
The amount of water used to grow it
The number of additives it contains
The land area needed to farm it
questions.explain: A carbon footprint measures the total greenhouse gas emissions associated with a food throughout its life.

questions.q: Why does buying locally grown, seasonal vegetables generally reduce environmental impact?
options: They need less transport and artificial heating, lowering greenhouse gas emissions
They always contain more vitamins than imported vegetables
They can never be grown organically
They require far more packaging to sell
questions.explain: Local, seasonal produce travels shorter distances and avoids heated greenhouses, reducing emissions and food miles.

questions.q: What does the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) logo on fish indicate?
options: The fish comes from a sustainable, well-managed source
The fish is guaranteed to be organic
The fish has been frozen at sea
The fish contains no bones
questions.explain: The MSC certifies that fish is caught using sustainable methods that protect fish stocks and the marine environment.

questions.q: Which statement best describes organic farming?
options: It restricts artificial pesticides and fertilisers, using natural methods instead
It uses the maximum possible amount of chemical fertiliser
It only applies to imported foods
It genetically modifies all crops to increase yield
questions.explain: Organic farming limits synthetic chemicals and relies on natural methods, aiming to be more environmentally sustainable.

questions.q: Why does buying Fairtrade products benefit farmers in developing countries?
options: It guarantees them a fair, stable price for their produce
It removes all import taxes on their goods
It means their crops are grown without any water
It guarantees the food is organic
questions.explain: Fairtrade ensures producers receive a fair and reliable price, improving their income and working conditions.

questions.q: A shopper in the UK in June wants the most environmentally sustainable option for a salad. Which should they choose?
options: Locally grown outdoor lettuce and tomatoes in season
Salad leaves air-freighted from another continent
Tomatoes grown in a heated greenhouse in winter
Pre-packed salad in single-use plastic imported by air
questions.explain: Local, in-season produce grown outdoors has the lowest food miles and energy use, so the smallest environmental impact.

questions.q: What is meant by 'food security'?
options: When people have reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
When food is locked in secure storage
When food is free from all additives
When a country exports more food than it imports
questions.explain: Food security means everyone has consistent access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active, healthy life.

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely to threaten a country's food security?
options: Climate change causing droughts and failed harvests
An increase in the number of supermarkets
Improved refrigeration in homes
A wider variety of imported foods
questions.explain: Extreme weather from climate change can destroy crops and reduce supply, threatening access to enough food.

questions.q: Which action would most effectively reduce food waste in the home?
options: Planning meals and using foods before their use-by date
Buying larger quantities than needed to save trips
Throwing away food on the best-before date without checking
Storing all foods at room temperature
questions.explain: Meal planning and using food before it spoils prevents edible food from being thrown away unnecessarily.

questions.q: A household has vegetable peelings and fruit cores left after cooking. What is the most sustainable way to deal with them?
options: Compost them so they return nutrients to the soil
Put them straight into general landfill waste
Pour them down the kitchen sink
Burn them in the garden
questions.explain: Composting recycles food scraps into nutrient-rich material for soil, diverting waste from landfill.

questions.q: What is 'primary processing' of food?
options: Turning a raw harvested or slaughtered material into a food or ingredient ready for use
Combining several ingredients into a ready meal
Adding flavourings and colourings to a finished product
Packaging food for supermarket shelves
questions.explain: Primary processing changes a raw material into an edible food or ingredient, such as milling wheat or washing vegetables.

questions.q: What is 'secondary processing' of food?
options: Changing a primary-processed food into another food product
Growing and harvesting a crop
Slaughtering an animal for meat
Cleaning soil off freshly dug potatoes
questions.explain: Secondary processing converts primary-processed ingredients into new products, for example flour into bread.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of PRIMARY processing?
options: Milling wheat grains into flour
Baking flour into bread
Making milk into cheese
Turning tomatoes into ketchup
questions.explain: Milling wheat into flour changes a raw harvested crop into a usable ingredient, so it is primary processing.

questions.q: A dairy takes milk and turns it into cheese and yoghurt. How should this be classified?
options: Secondary processing, because milk is made into a different product
Primary processing, because milk is a raw material
Neither, because no heat is used
Both are examples of harvesting
questions.explain: Milk is a primary-processed food, so turning it into cheese or yoghurt is secondary processing.

questions.q: What does 'fortification' of a food mean?
options: Adding nutrients such as vitamins or minerals to a food
Removing all the fat from a food
Sealing a food in airtight packaging
Freezing a food to preserve it
questions.explain: Fortification is the addition of nutrients to food, for example adding vitamins and minerals to flour or breakfast cereal.

questions.q: By UK law, white and brown flour must be fortified with which nutrients?
options: Calcium, iron, thiamin (B1) and niacin (B3)
Vitamin C, vitamin D and potassium
Protein, fibre and sugar
Sodium, chloride and vitamin A
questions.explain: UK law requires non-wholemeal flour to be fortified with calcium, iron, thiamin and niacin to replace nutrients lost in milling.

questions.q: Why can processing and cooking reduce the vitamin C content of vegetables?
options: Vitamin C is water-soluble and easily destroyed by heat
Vitamin C is only found in the packaging
Vitamin C is a fat and melts away when heated
Vitamin C is added back during freezing
questions.explain: Vitamin C dissolves in cooking water and is damaged by heat, so processing can lower the amount in food.

questions.q: A cook wants to retain the most vitamin C when preparing broccoli. Which method is best?
options: Steam it briefly rather than boiling it for a long time
Boil it in plenty of water for 20 minutes
Leave it chopped and soaking in water overnight
Fry it slowly in oil for a long period
questions.explain: Short steaming limits contact with water and heat, so less water-soluble vitamin C is lost.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of adding a preservative to a processed food?
options: To extend its shelf life and slow spoilage
To increase its sugar content
To improve its colour only
To reduce the price of the ingredients
questions.explain: Preservatives slow the growth of micro-organisms and spoilage, keeping food safe and edible for longer.
